messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Michael is a 34-year-old firefighter, married for eight years, who sought help after a year of escalating distress following his deployment as a relief worker in a war-torn region. The event that fractured his sense of safety happened on his third week there. He was part of a team distributing supplies in a contested neighborhood when a mortar round struck a building fifty feet away. In the chaos that followed, a young boy ran toward him, screaming, and Michael instinctively grabbed him and pulled him behind a wall—only to watch a second round land exactly where the boy had been standing. The boy survived, but Michael carried him to the aid station with blood streaming from a shrapnel wound. In the months since returning home, that moment has never left him.

Back in his daily life, Michael finds himself unable to shake the hypervigilance that kept him alive overseas. At the fire station, he sits with his back to the wall and scans the room for exits before he can focus on a conversation. At home, he feels on guard even inside his own house, his eyes darting to windows and doors whenever his wife moves through a room. Strangers approaching him in ordinary situations—a cashier leaning forward to hand him change, a jogger passing on the sidewalk—trigger a jolt of alertness that he cannot rationalize away. He has come to believe that danger is always one misstep away, and that letting his guard down will cost someone their life.

To manage this constant sense of threat, Michael has developed a set of habits that have slowly reshaped his life. He avoids exercise because the raised heart rate and breathlessness feel too close to the panic he felt during the attack, and he worries that losing control of his body in that way will make him vulnerable. He pushes away positive emotions, refusing to let himself feel joy or contentment, because those feelings feel unsafe—he is certain that the moment he relaxes, something terrible will happen. As soon as he enters any room or building, he scans for exits, and he makes sure to stay close to one at all times, often choosing seats near doors even if it means sitting apart from his crew. His wife has noticed that he no longer laughs at her jokes, and he has stopped going to the gym with his colleagues, offering vague excuses about being tired.

These strategies, however, have only deepened his sense of threat. By avoiding exercise and positive feelings, he has cut himself off from the very experiences that might have helped him recalibrate his nervous system. Staying near exits and scanning rooms reinforces his belief that danger is imminent, because each time he checks a door, he is reminding himself that he might need to flee. The more he avoids, the more vigilant he becomes, and the more vigilant he becomes, the more he feels the need to avoid. This cycle has tightened over the past year, leaving him exhausted and isolated.

What finally brought Michael to seek help was a moment at the fire station last month. A new recruit clapped him on the shoulder from behind, and Michael spun around with his fists raised, his heart pounding, before he realized where he was. The look of shock on the young man's face stayed with him. His wife had been urging him to see someone for months, but it was that moment—seeing himself through another person's eyes, recognizing how far he had drifted from the man he used to be—that made him pick up the phone. He is afraid of what he might become if this continues, but he is also afraid that letting go of his vigilance will mean letting someone get hurt. He hopes therapy can help him find a way to live without the constant weight of that fear.
